note: All story, chat, hint, card and debrief text. Story beats: max 12 words each, under 300 words in total. Story plus chat: under 650 words. The science event, teacher and crew are fictional. Sara Seager and Chris Hadfield are named as inspiration only: no portraits, no quotes, no endorsement.

story.text: You are a 10-year-old kid in Mississauga, Ontario.
After school, you build cities in strategy games.
At a science fair, you hear about two people from Ontario.
Chris Hadfield, a Canadian astronaut, commanded the Space Station.
Sara Seager, born in Toronto, studies planets around other stars.
You wonder: could I build a home on the Moon?
So you draw a Moon base.
The Lab and Rover Garage must wait. Power and people first.
Your teacher says: A civilization needs more than buildings.
It needs people, resources, science and a plan.
You grow up and study astronomy.
You earn a PhD. You never stop asking questions.
You train as an astronaut. This is a dream, not a promise.
Launch day! The Moon is waiting.
I drew this when I was ten. It is missing things.
Commander, your crew is ready. Build them a home.
Radio from a class in Mississauga: How do you breathe?
Good question. Air Support makes the air we breathe.
A long shadow is coming. Less sun means less power.
First harvest! The crew shares fresh greens.
Mission control: solar particle warning. The Sun still shines.
Yuki is outside, far from base.
Particles are here. Keep the crew in a powered Shelter.
All clear. The storm has passed.
The crew gathers at the window.
Sunlight creeps over the ridge. Solar power climbs.
Earth hangs low above the horizon.
Priya hands you an old photo: your first drawing.
I used to build this world on a computer.
Now we are building it together.
On Earth, a new kid opens Blueprint v2.
Yuki walks out to study old rocks.
Mission control: the Sun is very active.
Years later, a new rocket waits.
Next stop: Mars.
We land at Jezero crater. Long ago, it held a lake.

chat.line: Power is like water in a tank. Never let it empty.

replies.answer: Switch off what can wait. Air never waits.

chat.line: The battery is draining. Something must switch off.

replies.answer: The Greenhouse can rest. Air Support cannot.

chat.line: Two batteries! Now we can save energy for later.
The Shelter needs extra power. Check the battery now.

replies.answer: No. A warning is not a power cut.

chat.line: My seeds need soil, light, water and power.
Look, tiny sprouts! We recycle most of their water.

replies.answer: Water is hard to bring here. Every drop counts.

chat.line: First harvest! Real food, grown on the Moon.
Short on power? Let my plants rest. People come first.

replies.answer: Plants can wait a few hours. We cannot.

chat.line: These rocks are older than any city on Earth.

replies.answer: Maybe ice, hiding in the dark craters.

chat.line: My rover found soft soil for Mateo.

replies.answer: Ice in dark craters. Clay on Mars.

chat.line: I am far from base. Should I come back?

replies.answer: Okay. Call me if it gets worse.

chat.line: Safe inside. Thank you for watching over us.
You called me in first. I will not forget that.

replies.answer: That is why we follow you.

chat.line: That storm was scary. Call me sooner next time?

hints.text: Pick a building card below. Then click the map.
Place the Habitat first. Your base grows around it.
Build inside the lit area around your Habitat.
Time is running. Press Pause any time to think.
Brighter ground gets more sun. Put Solar Arrays there.
Put Batteries next to Solar Arrays. Long cables waste power.
Build it near soft soil and water. Short trips are faster.
Power in must beat power out. Watch the top bar.
Click a building to see what helps it.
Short on power? Switch the Greenhouse off for a while.
Next: Air Support, next to the Habitat. It makes air for the crew.
Next: Solar Arrays on bright ground. Everything needs power.
Next: a Battery within 2 tiles of your Solar Arrays.
Next: a Radio Dish, so you can call your crew.
Next: a Rover Garage near soil and water. Its rover fetches soil.
Next: the Greenhouse, next to Air Support. It needs 6 soil.
Power out is bigger than power in! Add a Solar Array or switch something off.
Green glowing tiles are good spots. They are tips, not rules.

cards.title: A low Sun
cards.text: At the Moon's poles, the Sun never climbs more than 1.5 degrees high.
cards.text2: So panels go on high, bright ground. Brighter tiles here make more power.
cards.source: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, south-pole shadows
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Place a Solar Array at a Moon base.

cards.title: No spot is always sunny
cards.text: On a real south-pole map, our sunniest spot is lit 71% of the time.
cards.text2: Even the best ridge has dark hours. Batteries carry the base through them.
cards.source: LRO LOLA average illumination map (Mazarico et al. 2011, Icarus 211), our 20 x 15 crop
cards.label: simplified from real map
cards.hint: Place a Battery at a Moon base.

cards.title: Long shadows
cards.text: On NASA's polar map, some crater floors see sunlight under 4% of the time.
cards.text2: The map was worked out from heights measured by LRO's LOLA laser.
cards.source: LRO LOLA average illumination map (Mazarico et al. 2011, Icarus 211), our 20 x 15 crop
cards.label: simplified from real map
cards.hint: Keep a Moon base running through a long shadow.

cards.title: Ice in the dark
cards.text: Some craters near the Moon's poles never see the Sun. They can trap ice.
cards.text2: In 2009, NASA's LCROSS found water ice in one, called Cabeus.
cards.source: NASA NSSDC, Ice on the Moon
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build a Rover Garage at a Moon base.

cards.title: Sun at home
cards.text: Back home in Mississauga, June brings about five times more sun energy than December.
cards.text2: NASA POWER: June gets about 6.1 kWh per square metre daily; December 1.2.
cards.source: NASA POWER climatology, Mississauga, 2001 to 2025
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Watch the Moon sunrise at the end of the Solar Storm mission.

cards.title: Less sunlight on Mars
cards.text: Sunlight on Mars is about 43% as strong as on Earth.
cards.text2: So a Mars base needs more panels for the same power.
cards.source: NASA NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet
cards.label: NASA-derived; game power is softened
cards.hint: Place a Solar Array on Mars.

cards.title: A Mars day
cards.text: A Mars day, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes.
cards.text2: Panels rest at night, so batteries matter. This game skips Mars nights.
cards.source: NASA NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Place a Battery on Mars.

cards.title: Making oxygen from Mars air
cards.text: Mars air is 95% carbon dioxide. NASA's MOXIE made oxygen from it.
cards.text2: At its best it made 12 grams an hour, and 122 grams in all.
cards.source: NASA JPL, MOXIE completes Mars mission (6 Sept 2023); NASA NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build Air Support on Mars.

cards.title: Jezero crater
cards.text: NASA's Perseverance landed in Jezero crater in 2021. It once held a lake.
cards.text2: This map uses real heights from the MOLA laser on Mars Global Surveyor.
cards.source: NASA JPL Mars 2020 press kit; MGS MOLA MEGDR (NASA PDS)
cards.label: simplified from real map
cards.hint: Build a Rover Garage on Mars.

cards.title: Dust storms
cards.text: In 2018, a Mars-wide dust storm covered NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover.
cards.text2: Built for 90 Mars days, it worked for over 15 years before going silent.
cards.source: NASA news release, Opportunity mission comes to end (13 Feb 2019)
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Keep a Mars base running through a dust storm.

cards.title: Making air
cards.text: The Space Station makes oxygen by splitting water into oxygen and hydrogen.
cards.text2: It also cleans and reuses about 90% of its water.
cards.source: NASA, Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (updated 4 April 2025)
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build Air Support at a Moon base.

cards.title: Talking across space
cards.text: A radio call reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds.
cards.text2: From Mars, one way can take more than 20 minutes.
cards.source: NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet (384,400 km at the speed of light); NASA Moon to Mars white paper (2023)
cards.label: NASA-derived; Moon time worked out
cards.hint: Build a Radio Dish.

cards.title: Tiny space rocks
cards.text: Photos of the Space Station show thousands of hits from tiny space particles.
cards.text2: Engineers keep testing better shields to protect spacecraft.
cards.source: NASA Johnson, Hypervelocity Impact Technology team
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Play Free Build on Normal or Hard, and wait for a space rock.

cards.title: Space salad
cards.text: Space Station crews have grown lettuce, mizuna mustard and dwarf tomatoes.
cards.text2: Scientists checked the space lettuce for germs and nutrients.
cards.source: NASA Veg-04 and Veg-05 investigation page; NASA OSDR studies OSD-268 and OSD-767
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build a Greenhouse.

cards.title: A Canadian space gardener
cards.text: Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques filled the water tank of a space plant system.
cards.text2: It was the Veggie PONDS system, on the International Space Station.
cards.source: Canadian Space Agency, Growing healthy food in space (photo caption). © Canadian Space Agency
cards.label: CSA-derived
cards.hint: Grow food in the Greenhouse until your first harvest.

cards.title: Why grow plants in space?
cards.text: Plants can provide food, produce oxygen, and recycle carbon dioxide.
cards.text2: Over three million students took part in Tomatosphere from 2001 to 2016.
cards.source: Canadian Space Agency, Tomatosphere. © Canadian Space Agency
cards.label: CSA-derived
cards.hint: At a first harvest, press the Why plants? button.

cards.title: Far from the grocery store
cards.text: On the Moon or Mars, astronauts will need to be more self-sufficient.
cards.text2: Supply trips will be rare, so crews must grow food.
cards.source: Canadian Space Agency, Growing healthy food in space. © Canadian Space Agency
cards.label: CSA-derived
cards.hint: Wait for a supply lander to arrive.

cards.title: Staying strong
cards.text: Bodies lose muscle and bone in space. Mice on the Station helped study it.
cards.text2: One study tested a way to protect them: OSDR study OSD-342.
cards.source: NASA Open Science Data Repository, OSD-342
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build a Habitat for your crew.

cards.title: Why shelter?
cards.text: Space radiation comes from the Sun's particles and from cosmic rays.
cards.text2: It can damage DNA inside our cells. Shielding helps protect the crew.
cards.source: NASA Human Research Program, About the Space Radiation Element (31 July 2024)
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Build a Shelter.

cards.title: A radiation alarm
cards.text: A NASA sensor called HERA can warn crews to take shelter from solar flares.
cards.text2: It flew inside Orion on Artemis I, alongside 5,600 small passive sensors.
cards.source: NASA, Artemis I radiation measurements validate Orion safety (9 Oct 2024); George et al. 2024, Nature 634, 48-52
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Get your first solar storm warning.

cards.title: A real reading from the Space Station
cards.text: On 11 May 2024, a Space Station sensor read about {issMedian} microgray an hour.
cards.text2: The highest was {issMax}. Station readings are not Moon doses.
cards.source: NASA OSDR RadLab, ISS DosTel, 11 May 2024, 00:00 to 06:00 UTC
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Stay safe until your first storm's particles arrive.

cards.title: A fast cloud
cards.text: This storm's real cloud of solar gas flew at {speed} km per second.
cards.text2: That fast, it could cross from Earth to the Moon in {moonMinutes} minutes.
cards.source: NASA CCMC DONKI (CME analysis); NASA NSSDC Moon Fact Sheet
cards.label: NASA-derived; time worked out
cards.hint: Get a second solar storm warning.

cards.title: Particles arrive
cards.text: Real data: fast particles were logged {sepDelay} after the flare's peak.
cards.text2: Our 8 real storms ranged from 16 minutes to almost 3 days.
cards.source: NASA CCMC DONKI (linked SEP events)
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Stay safe until a second storm's particles arrive.

cards.title: Storm on Earth
cards.text: Around this storm, Earth's Kp storm scale reached {kp}. It tops out at 9.
cards.text2: Strong storms on Earth can paint the sky with auroras.
cards.source: NASA CCMC DONKI (geomagnetic storm); NASA Science, the most intense solar storm in decades (16 May 2024)
cards.label: NASA-derived
cards.hint: Keep your crew safe until a solar storm is over.
